missions.name: Salvation Army and Holiness missions (Booth, Booth-Tucker in India, Keswick)
missions.statusNote: The Salvation Army works in more than 130 countries and is one of the world’s largest non-governmental providers of social services; its evangelistic and social wings remain intertwined. Holiness denominations (Nazarenes, Wesleyans, Free Methodists, the Christian and Missionary Alliance) continue as international churches whose membership is now mostly outside North America, while the Keswick Convention survives as an annual Bible-teaching gathering rather than a missionary engine.
missions.summary: A cluster of nineteenth-century movements, rooted in Methodist teaching on entire sanctification and in the ‘higher life’ spirituality of Keswick, that turned holiness piety into a missionary force. William and Catherine Booth’s Salvation Army carried a uniformed, quasi-military evangelism and social work from the East End of London to India, Africa, Asia and the Americas; Frederick Booth-Tucker adopted Indian dress and begging bowls in Bombay. Keswick sent a stream of volunteers into the CMS and faith missions, and American holiness churches built their own mission networks.
missions.story:
The holiness movement grew out of John Wesley’s teaching that believers could be made perfect in love in this life. In the United States Phoebe Palmer’s ‘altar theology’ (1830s–1870s) made entire sanctification an instantaneous, attainable experience, and camp meetings of the National Camp Meeting Association (from 1867) spread it across Methodism. In Britain the American lay preachers Robert Pearsall Smith and Hannah Whitall Smith led ‘higher life’ meetings at Broadlands and Oxford (1874) and Brighton (1875), and the vicar of Keswick, T. D. Harford-Battersby, began the Keswick Convention in 1875. Keswick taught a less Wesleyan, ‘counteraction’ view of victory over sin, but shared the conviction that a consecrated life should be poured out in service — and from the 1880s that increasingly meant overseas mission.

William Booth, a former Methodist New Connexion minister, began open-air preaching in Whitechapel in 1865 with his wife Catherine, a forceful advocate of women’s preaching. The East London Christian Mission was renamed The Salvation Army in 1878; it adopted ranks, uniforms, flags, brass bands and a ‘General’, and in 1883 stopped celebrating baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Its rowdy processions provoked the ‘Skeleton Army’ riots in English towns and bans in Switzerland, but it grew fast. George Scott Railton and seven women ‘lasses’ opened work in New York in 1880; officers reached Australia (1880), France and Canada (1881–82), India, Sweden and Switzerland (1882), South Africa, Ceylon and New Zealand (1883), and later Japan (1895), Korea (1908), Nigeria (1920), Kenya (1921), the Gold Coast (1922) and the Belgian Congo (1934). Booth’s In Darkest England and the Way Out (1890), drafted with W. T. Stead, set out a scheme of shelters, labour bureaux and farm colonies that defined the Army’s social mission.

India was its most distinctive experiment. Frederick Tucker, a former Indian Civil Service officer, landed at Bombay in September 1882 with three companions. The party wore Indian dress, went barefoot, took Indian names (Tucker became ‘Fakir Singh’), lived on alms and preached in the vernacular, a deliberate imitation of the sadhu that won attention among villagers in Gujarat, Punjab and the south but also arrests in Bombay for street processions. Tucker married Booth’s daughter Emma in 1888 and took the name Booth-Tucker. On his return to lead the Indian work (1907–1919) the Army took on a role that has since attracted sharp criticism: from 1908 it managed settlements for communities labelled ‘criminal tribes’ under the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, running agricultural and industrial colonies in the United Provinces, Punjab and Madras on behalf of the colonial state.

Keswick’s missionary influence ran through other bodies. The ‘Cambridge Seven’ who joined the China Inland Mission in 1885 were steeped in its piety; the Keswick missionary meeting (from 1886) and the ‘Keswick missioner’ scheme sent people such as Amy Carmichael (to Japan in 1893 and India in 1895) and shaped the CMS ‘Keswick men’ on the Niger in the late 1880s. In America the holiness churches organised their own missions: the Christian and Missionary Alliance (A. B. Simpson, 1887), the Church of the Nazarene (united at Pilot Point, Texas, in 1908), the Free Methodists and Wesleyan Methodists, and the Oriental Missionary Society of Charles and Lettie Cowman and Ernest Kilbourne, which began in Tokyo in 1901 and grew into the Korea Evangelical Holiness Church after 1907.

The holiness emphasis on a second, crisis experience of the Spirit fed directly into Pentecostalism after 1901, and many holiness congregations, especially in the American South and in India, became Pentecostal; others reacted strongly against tongues. In the twentieth century the Salvation Army increasingly became known as a relief and welfare agency — hostels, disaster response, addiction services, hospitals such as Catherine Booth Hospital in Nagercoil (1893) — while still describing itself as an evangelical church. It has faced institutional-abuse findings in children’s homes, notably before Australia’s Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (2014–15), and recurring controversy over its teaching on sexuality.

The holiness missions left large churches in the global South: by the early twenty-first century most Salvationists lived in Africa and Asia, with India, Kenya, Zimbabwe, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Papua New Guinea among its largest territories, and the Church of the Nazarene and the C&MA reported a majority of members outside the United States. Historians credit the movement with pioneering women’s public ministry and with fusing evangelism to practical social care, while noting its paternalism and its readiness to serve imperial governments.
beliefs: Entire sanctification or ‘full salvation’: a second work of grace, after conversion, cleansing the heart and enabling a life of perfect love (Wesleyan holiness, Salvation Army)
Keswick ‘higher life’ teaching: victory over known sin by continual surrender and faith, without the claim that the sinful nature is eradicated
Holiness expressed in service: consecration was expected to lead to evangelism, rescue work and overseas mission
Equality of women in ministry: Catherine Booth’s Female Ministry (1859) and Salvation Army practice gave women officers equal rank in preaching and command
Non-observance of baptism and the Lord’s Supper in the Salvation Army (from 1883), holding that inward grace does not depend on outward rites
Strong conversionist urgency combined with belief that social salvation (‘soup, soap and salvation’) was part of the gospel
strategies: Military organisation: territories, corps, ranks, uniforms, flags and brass bands to attract attention and build discipline
Open-air preaching, street processions and ‘invasions’ of new towns by small teams of officers
Identification with the poor: Booth-Tucker’s team in India adopted Indian dress, names, bare feet and begging
Social institutions: shelters, rescue homes for women, labour colonies, hospitals, leprosy work and disaster relief
Conventions and consecration meetings (Keswick, National Camp Meeting Association) that recruited missionaries
Self-funded denominational boards for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan, Free Methodist, C&MA) sending missionaries alongside national evangelists
groupsReached: The urban poor, alcoholics and prostitutes of industrial Britain, the United States and Australia
Rural and low-caste communities in Gujarat, Punjab and Tamil Nadu, including Dalits and communities labelled ‘criminal tribes’
Japanese and Korean urban populations through the Oriental Missionary Society (Korea Evangelical Holiness Church)
Communities in southern and eastern Africa — Zimbabwe, Kenya, Zambia, Congo — where the Salvation Army became a large church
Indigenous and Caribbean peoples served by the C&MA, Nazarene and Wesleyan missions in Latin America
Lepers, orphans and displaced people through medical and relief institutions
challenges: Mob violence and legal bans: the ‘Skeleton Army’ riots in England (1880s), expulsions from Swiss cantons, arrests in Bombay (1882–83)
Disease and early deaths among officers living in Indian style on alms
Tension between evangelistic aims and the growing weight of social and relief institutions
Holiness divisions over tongues after 1906, which split congregations and missions
Dependence on colonial authorities for land, grants and permission to operate
Financial strain and authoritarian governance under a single General, leading to schisms (e.g. Ballington and Maud Booth’s Volunteers of America, 1896)
harms: In India the Salvation Army administered ‘criminal tribe’ settlements for the colonial government (from 1908), participating in a system of surveillance, restricted movement and compulsory labour imposed on whole communities
Paternalism: officers from Britain long monopolised senior command in mission territories, and indigenous leadership was slow to be promoted
Abuse of children in Salvation Army homes in Australia, Canada and Britain, documented by public inquiries in the 2000s–2010s
Holiness perfectionism produced cases of spiritual pressure, guilt and harsh discipline, and some rejection of medicine in faith-healing wings
Clashes with local religious communities and with other churches over aggressive street evangelism and ‘sheep-stealing’
developments: Pioneered large-scale equality of women in preaching and leadership decades before most denominations
Built a worldwide network of hostels, hospitals, schools, leprosy and disaster-relief services
Booth-Tucker’s adoption of Indian dress and lifestyle was an early Protestant experiment in identification with local culture
Keswick spirituality shaped generations of evangelical missionaries, including the Cambridge Seven and Amy Carmichael
Holiness churches in Korea, Japan, Africa and Latin America became self-governing national churches
The holiness ‘second blessing’ framework supplied the theological seedbed for Pentecostalism
missions.outcome: The holiness missions produced international churches whose centre of gravity has shifted to Africa, Asia and Latin America, and made the Salvation Army a global welfare institution. Their pairing of personal holiness with social action endured, as did criticism of their colonial entanglements and institutional failures.

keyPeople.name: William Booth
keyPeople.role: Founder and first General of The Salvation Army
keyPeople.focus: Urban evangelism and social schemes (In Darkest England, 1890)
keyPeople.outcome: Left an Army operating in some 58 countries at his death

keyPeople.name: Catherine Booth
keyPeople.role: Co-founder, preacher and theologian of the Army
keyPeople.focus: Women’s right to preach; holiness teaching
keyPeople.outcome: Her Female Ministry (1859) underpinned the Army’s equal-rank policy

keyPeople.name: Frederick Booth-Tucker
keyPeople.role: Leader of the Salvation Army in India
keyPeople.focus: Indian-style evangelism; later the ‘criminal tribe’ settlements
keyPeople.outcome: Built the Indian work into one of the Army’s largest territories

keyPeople.name: Hannah Whitall Smith
keyPeople.focus: The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life (1875)
keyPeople.outcome: Her Brighton and Oxford meetings led to the Keswick Convention

keyPeople.name: A. B. Simpson
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Christian and Missionary Alliance
keyPeople.focus: The ‘Fourfold Gospel’ and sending missionaries to unreached fields
keyPeople.outcome: C&MA became a major mission in Asia, Africa and Latin America

keyPeople.name: Charles and Lettie Cowman
keyPeople.role: Co-founders of the Oriental Missionary Society
keyPeople.focus: Bible training of Japanese and Korean evangelists
keyPeople.outcome: Their work produced the Korea Evangelical Holiness Church

countries.text: The Christian Mission in Whitechapel became The Salvation Army in 1878; Keswick (from 1875) became the leading British holiness convention.
George Scott Railton and seven women opened work in New York; the US later became the Army’s largest social-service operation and the base of the holiness denominations.
Work began in Adelaide; the Army became a major welfare provider, later investigated for abuse in its boys’ homes.
Catherine Booth-Clibborn (‘La Maréchale’) led the work in Paris amid hostility.
Frederick Tucker’s party landed in Bombay in Indian dress; the Army grew among rural and Dalit communities and ran ‘criminal tribe’ settlements from 1908.
Officers opened work in Colombo as an extension of the Indian campaign.
The Army began in Cape Town and spread into Zimbabwe (1891) and the wider region.
The Army campaigned against licensed prostitution under Gunpei Yamamuro; the Oriental Missionary Society began in Tokyo in 1901.
The Oriental Missionary Society’s work became the Korea Evangelical Holiness Church; the Salvation Army arrived in 1908.
The Army grew into one of its largest African territories, with schools and medical work.
Work began in Kinshasa (then Léopoldville) and became a large church and social presence.

journeys.title: Railton and the seven ‘lasses’ invade New York
journeys.people: George Scott Railton and seven women officers
journeys.text: Railton’s party landed in March 1880 and held their first meeting in Manhattan, opening the Army’s American work.

journeys.title: Frederick Tucker’s party to Bombay
journeys.text: The party arrived in September 1882, adopted Indian dress and names, and were soon arrested for holding street processions.

relations.text: Holiness teaching on a second, crisis experience of the Spirit and holiness networks (Parham, Seymour, Garr, Mukti) were the direct seedbed of Pentecostalism.
Keswick spirituality supplied many faith-mission recruits, including the Cambridge Seven (1885).
Keswick-influenced CMS missionaries (the ‘Keswick men’ on the Niger, 1887–90) carried higher-life piety into Anglican mission.

agreements.text: Shared the Wesleyan doctrine of Christian perfection and Arminian evangelism.
Shared Keswick spirituality, conversionist urgency and willingness to send lay men and women.

disagreements.text: Many holiness churches (e.g. the Nazarenes, who dropped ‘Pentecostal’ from their name in 1919) rejected speaking in tongues as the evidence of Spirit baptism.
The Salvation Army’s non-sacramental practice complicated its place in ecumenical bodies; it left full WCC membership in 1981 after controversy over the Programme to Combat Racism.

deviations: The Salvation Army abandoned baptism and the Lord’s Supper (1883), departing from the practice of nearly every other Christian church
Its Indian ‘criminal tribe’ settlements made a movement for the outcast an instrument of colonial control
Over time the social-service wing came to overshadow the original revivalist mission in many Western countries

missions.name: Azusa Street and the Pentecostal missionary explosion (Garr, Assemblies of God, global Pentecostalism)
missions.statusNote: Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is the fastest-growing form of Christianity of the past century; the World Christian Database estimates well over 600 million adherents in the 2020s, though totals depend heavily on how ‘charismatic’ is defined. Most adherents live in Africa, Latin America and Asia and belong to nationally founded churches rather than missions.
missions.summary: Beginning with Charles Parham’s Bible school in Topeka (1901) and William J. Seymour’s Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906–09), Pentecostals taught that Spirit baptism, evidenced by speaking in tongues, empowered believers for world evangelisation before Christ’s imminent return. Within a few years missionaries had gone from Azusa Street and its satellite revivals to India, China, Africa, Scandinavia and South America, and the Assemblies of God (1914) built one of the largest mission organisations of the century. The movement’s later explosive growth was driven above all by indigenous preachers.
missions.story:
Pentecostalism was missionary from the start. At Charles Fox Parham’s Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901, and Parham taught that this gift was xenolalia — real foreign languages bestowed so that missionaries could preach abroad without study. In Houston in 1905 Parham’s segregated classes were attended, from the corridor, by William J. Seymour, an African American holiness preacher. Seymour carried the message to Los Angeles, and from April 1906 the Apostolic Faith Mission at 312 Azusa Street drew black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers in meetings that ran almost continuously until about 1909. Its paper, The Apostolic Faith, sent free to tens of thousands of readers, reported that ‘Pentecost has come’ and announced missionaries leaving for the ends of the earth.

The first wave of ‘missionaries of the one-way ticket’ left within months. Alfred G. Garr and Lillian Garr, believing they had received Bengali and Chinese, sailed for India and reached Calcutta at the end of 1906; finding that their tongues were not intelligible, they preached in English among missionaries and Anglo-Indians, helped spread Pentecostal experience in missionary circles, and went on to Hong Kong in 1907. Others went to Liberia, Angola and China. The disappointment of xenolalia led most Pentecostals to reinterpret tongues as prayer languages, but the conviction of empowerment for mission remained. Revivals elsewhere — the Welsh revival (1904–05), Pandita Ramabai’s Mukti Mission near Pune (1905), and the Korean revival (1907) — showed that the movement had multiple origins.

The experience spread by networks of holiness and evangelical periodicals. The Methodist Thomas Ball Barratt, having received Spirit baptism in New York, brought it to Kristiania (Oslo) in December 1906, and from there it reached Sweden (Lewi Pethrus’s Filadelfia church, Stockholm), Britain (Alexander Boddy in Sunderland, 1907) and Germany. Swedish Baptists Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, influenced in Chicago by William Durham, landed at Belém in November 1910; their split from the local Baptist church in 1911 began what became the Assembleias de Deus, now Brazil’s largest Protestant church. Willis Hoover’s Methodist congregation in Valparaíso experienced revival in 1909, producing the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile. In South Africa John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch founded the Apostolic Faith Mission in 1908, whose Zionist offshoots fed into African independent churches.

Organisation followed. The Church of God in Christ (C. H. Mason, 1907) and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) became Pentecostal; the Assemblies of God was founded at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914, with a strong emphasis on foreign missions, and adopted Roland Allen-style ‘indigenous church’ principles, systematised by Melvin Hodges in The Indigenous Church (1953). The Oneness controversy split the movement in 1916, and racial division hardened: the Assemblies of God was overwhelmingly white, and the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (1948) excluded black churches until its dissolution and replacement in the ‘Memphis Miracle’ of 1994. British Pentecostals formed the Elim (1915) and Assemblies of God (1924) churches, with missions in Africa and India.

After 1945 the decisive growth came from national leaders and churches: the Church of Pentecost in Ghana (from James McKeown’s work, 1937), the Redeemed Christian Church of God (Nigeria, 1952), David Yonggi Cho’s Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul (1958), the Indian Pentecostal Church of God (1924) and Ceylon Pentecostal Mission, and Chinese house churches with strongly charismatic practice. Healing evangelists such as T. L. Osborn and Reinhard Bonnke drew vast crowds in Africa, while the charismatic renewal from 1960 carried Pentecostal experience into the historic Protestant and Catholic churches. Neo-Pentecostal megachurches, often teaching prosperity, multiplied in Latin America and Africa from the 1980s.

Scholars such as Allan Anderson and Walter Hollenweger argue that Pentecostalism’s growth owes most to its oral, participatory worship, its translation of the gospel into local idioms of spiritual power, healing and deliverance, and its openness to lay and women preachers. Critics point to the prosperity gospel, authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership, financial scandals, witchcraft accusations in deliverance ministries, and political alliances with strongmen. The movement now sends missionaries from Brazil, Nigeria, Korea and elsewhere throughout the world.
beliefs: Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, classically evidenced by speaking in tongues (the ‘initial evidence’ doctrine)
The ‘full gospel’: Jesus as saviour, sanctifier (in holiness Pentecostalism), Spirit-baptiser, healer and coming king
Divine healing and other spiritual gifts (prophecy, deliverance, miracles) as signs accompanying the preaching of the gospel
Urgent premillennial expectation of Christ’s return, making world evangelisation the task of the ‘latter rain’
Early belief that tongues were missionary languages (xenolalia), later reinterpreted as prayer and worship
Priesthood of all believers expressed in lay, women’s and young people’s ministry, though institutional churches later restricted women’s leadership
strategies: Independent ‘one-way ticket’ missionaries with little training or support, trusting divine provision
Spread through periodicals (The Apostolic Faith, Confidence, The Pentecostal Evangel) and networks of holiness missions
Healing campaigns and mass crusades emphasising signs and wonders
Indigenous-church principles: rapid training of national pastors and self-supporting churches (Hodges, AG Bible schools)
Lay evangelism by converts, open-air preaching and church planting in urban peripheries
Use of radio, television and later social media by national ministries
groupsReached: Working-class and migrant communities in the United States, including African Americans and Mexican Americans
The urban poor of Brazil, Chile, Guatemala and other Latin American countries
West African and southern African urban populations, through national churches and independent ministries
Dalit and tribal communities in Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Northeast India
Rural and urban believers in Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia and China
Members of mainline and Catholic churches through the charismatic renewal
challenges: Failure of xenolalia and lack of training left early missionaries stranded, sick or returning home
Doctrinal splits: finished-work vs holiness sanctification (1910s), the Oneness controversy (1916)
Racial segregation within the American movement
Opposition from holiness and fundamentalist leaders who called tongues demonic or delusional
Persecution by Catholic authorities in Latin America and state restrictions in China and elsewhere
Fragmentation into thousands of independent churches and ministries with weak accountability
harms: Racial division after the interracial beginnings at Azusa Street, institutionalised in white-only fellowships until 1994
Prosperity teaching that links giving to wealth and health has been criticised for exploiting poor congregations
Deliverance and witchcraft-accusation practices in some African churches have contributed to the abuse of children and elderly people
Financial and sexual scandals among televangelists and megachurch leaders
Denunciation of traditional religions and of other churches, sometimes provoking conflict
Authoritarian leadership cultures and alliances with authoritarian politicians in parts of Africa and Latin America
developments: Made Christianity a mass religion of the poor in Latin America and accelerated church growth in Africa and Asia
Opened leadership to lay people, the uneducated and (especially early) women
Created vigorous indigenous churches largely independent of Western control
Influenced all major traditions through the charismatic renewal, including Catholicism
Developed social ministries in education, rehabilitation and community development (documented by Miller and Yamamori)
Turned the global South into a major sender of missionaries
missions.outcome: Pentecostalism became the second-largest Christian grouping after Catholicism by many estimates, centred in the global South. Its missionary dynamism shifted from Western mission boards to national churches and transnational networks, carrying both renewal and controversy.

keyPeople.name: Charles Fox Parham
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Apostolic Faith movement
keyPeople.focus: Tongues as initial evidence and as missionary xenolalia
keyPeople.outcome: Discredited by scandal in 1907; his teaching shaped the movement

keyPeople.name: William J. Seymour
keyPeople.role: Pastor of the Azusa Street Mission
keyPeople.outcome: His mission became the movement’s symbolic centre

keyPeople.name: Alfred G. Garr
keyPeople.role: First Azusa Street missionary to Asia
keyPeople.outcome: Spread Pentecostal experience among missionaries; abandoned xenolalia theory

keyPeople.name: Thomas Ball Barratt
keyPeople.role: Methodist minister and Pentecostal pioneer in Europe
keyPeople.outcome: Seeded Pentecostalism in Scandinavia, Britain and Germany

keyPeople.name: Gunnar Vingren
keyPeople.role: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus
keyPeople.outcome: Brazilian AG grew into the country’s largest Protestant church

keyPeople.name: Daniel Berg
keyPeople.role: Co-founder of the Assembleias de Deus
keyPeople.outcome: Supported the work as a foundry worker and colporteur

keyPeople.name: Willis Hoover
keyPeople.outcome: Expelled by Methodists; founded the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile

keyPeople.name: David Yonggi Cho
keyPeople.role: Founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church
keyPeople.outcome: Built the world’s largest congregation; later convicted of embezzlement (2014)

countries.text: Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906) launched the movement; the Assemblies of God (1914) became a major sending body.
The Garrs arrived in Calcutta; Mukti revival (1905) and Kerala churches (IPC, 1924; Ceylon Pentecostal Mission) built an indigenous movement.
T. B. Barratt’s meetings in Kristiania made Oslo the gateway of European Pentecostalism.
Azusa missionaries and the Garrs worked in Hong Kong and south China; later indigenous groups (True Jesus Church, Jesus Family) and house churches adopted charismatic practice.
Alexander Boddy’s Sunderland conventions; Elim (1915) and Assemblies of God (1924) sent missionaries to Africa and India.
John G. Lake founded the Apostolic Faith Mission, whose Zionist offshoots influenced African independent churches.
The Valparaíso revival produced the Methodist Pentecostal Church, an early fully national Pentecostal church.
Berg and Vingren founded the Assembleias de Deus in Belém; Brazil became the largest Pentecostal country.
James McKeown’s work led to the Church of Pentecost, now a major sending church.
The Redeemed Christian Church of God and other national churches grew into transnational networks.
Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul grew to several hundred thousand members.

Pentecostalism began among missionaries and converts of the Primitive Methodist mission in the 1930s and grew rapidly from the 1960s; by the 2000s Protestants, most of them Pentecostal, were a large minority.

journeys.title: The Garrs from Azusa Street to Calcutta and Hong Kong
journeys.text: Expecting to preach in Bengali by miraculous gift, the Garrs found they could not; they ministered in English in Calcutta and then moved to Hong Kong, spreading Pentecostal experience among missionaries.

journeys.title: Barratt brings Pentecost to Europe
journeys.text: Barratt received Spirit baptism in New York while fund-raising, and his December 1906 meetings in Oslo spread the movement through northern Europe.

journeys.title: Berg and Vingren to Belém
journeys.text: Following a prophecy naming ‘Pará’, the two Swedes sailed from New York and arrived in Belém in November 1910, founding the Assembleias de Deus the next year.

journeys.title: John G. Lake to South Africa
journeys.people: John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch
journeys.text: Lake’s party drew on Zionist networks already in South Africa and founded the Apostolic Faith Mission.

relations.text: Chilean and Brazilian Pentecostal churches became the core of Latin American Protestant growth.
Apostolic Faith Mission and Pentecostal ideas shaped Zionist and Aladura churches, though these also had independent origins.
Korean Pentecostalism, especially Yoido Full Gospel Church, became a major engine of Korean missions.
Pentecostal churches in Nigeria, Brazil and Ghana became leading majority-world sending bodies.

agreements.text: Shared the holiness pattern of a post-conversion crisis experience and lay, women’s and working-class ministry.
Pentecostals increasingly joined evangelical bodies (NAE, 1942; Lausanne) and shared their priority on evangelism.

disagreements.text: Many fundamentalist and faith-mission leaders were cessationists who held that tongues and miracles had ceased with the apostles, and condemned Pentecostalism.
Most Pentecostals stayed outside the WCC and distrusted its theology, although some (e.g. Chilean churches, 1961) joined and dialogue began from the 1970s.

Church Growth writers studied Pentecostal growth admiringly, but Pentecostals disputed managerial, numerical approaches that downplayed the Spirit’s sovereignty — a gap partly closed by Wagner’s turn to ‘signs and wonders’.

deviations: The early xenolalia doctrine proved false and was quietly abandoned
The interracial, egalitarian vision of Azusa Street gave way within a decade to segregated denominations
Prosperity teaching departed from the early movement’s ascetic, other-worldly holiness piety
Restrictions on women’s ordination in many institutional Pentecostal churches reversed early practice
